output.title: Lantern published service alias rule — May 14 decision
output.body:
# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Authority-record time semantics — March 18 brown-bag

## Authoritative source time
`source_timestamp` represents the original authoritative time of the underlying authority record. Later observation, serialization, processing, retry, and navigation times may be recorded as separate metadata, but they must not replace or refresh `source_timestamp`.

## Fail-closed behavior
If a required source timestamp is missing or malformed, downstream navigation fails closed to explicit unknown.

## Multiple authority references
When one card carries multiple authority references, each reference retains its own `source_timestamp`. An envelope time, render time, processing time, or newest retry time must not be substituted for any reference's authoritative source time.

## Unchanged boundaries
This discussion creates no ownership, implementation, release, approval, or customer-authorization change. The internal reference-only integration remains outside the Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce customer paths.

## Example 1 — separate reassessment time from entry time

### What happened
A reassessment was completed at 16:55, and the entry documenting it was made at 17:40.

### Safe wording
“Late entry entered at 17:40 for a reassessment performed at 16:55. This entry records the findings from the 16:55 reassessment and does not alter the earlier record.”

That the entry existed at 16:55, that documentation time was changed to match the reassessment time, or that an earlier entry was replaced.

A later review found that the original entry omitted a clarification. The original entry remains visible, and an addendum is entered at 18:10.

“Addendum entered at 18:10: [clarification]. This addendum supplements the original entry; it does not replace or backdate it.”

That the original entry was changed or deleted, that the addendum existed before 18:10, or that the underlying care necessarily occurred at 18:10.

output.body:
# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The first run engaged the secondary at minute 47 while the cause remained unisolated, missing the required before-45-minute boundary. The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.

# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.
- 09:05 ET — p99 returned to about 46 ms, error rate returned to roughly 0.02%, and dropped writes returned to zero.

## What changed
The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

## Why rollback was appropriate
The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

## Follow-ups
1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.
2. Patch the Cardinality Guardrails checklist so live-path label value-shape changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture, not only replay validation.

## Non-goals
This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.

input.title: Training Appendix — April 18 Shard-Keeper Outage
input.body:
# Training Appendix: April 18 Shard-Keeper Outage

## What misled the investigation

The first investigation branch followed a network-layer explanation because the pages looked like generic ingest instability. That branch was plausible but misleading: symptom alerts fired, while the expected cause alerts remained silent. The decisive finding was the label-name diff—Nadia’s change reached `shard-keeper`, but `rollup-service` never picked it up. The rollback path was also fragile, so widening it under pressure risked making the incident worse.

## Confirmed data impact

- Ingestion was impaired for hours across essentially the incident window.
- The incident was treated as a Sev2; the path to fully clean was estimated at about 5 hours 45 minutes.
- Final review reported no data loss. During response, however, this had to remain an explicit validation item: “no evidence of data loss yet” was not equivalent to “no data loss confirmed.”

## Training takeaway

When symptoms and cause alerts disagree, inspect recent cross-service configuration and consumer parity before committing to an infrastructure explanation. Treat a label change as only shard-keeper-validated until `rollup-service` confirms the same name and semantics; keep a fragile rollback narrow, escalate promptly, and do not close the incident until ingestion recovery, backlog/error rates, and data integrity are verified.

Yes—retire the shorter leash immediately. A one-centimeter area with visibly cut load-bearing fibers is a structural failure in progress; trimming it or covering it with tape can hide further damage but cannot restore the webbing’s strength. Mark it “do not use” and replace it rather than testing it under tension.

Until then, the intact longer leash is the safer option, even though it is less convenient near the entrances:

- Before the walk, inspect its entire webbing, handle stitching, attachment point, and clasp. The clasp should close fully and consistently on its own; if it sticks, leaves a gap, or needs a push even once, do not use it.
- Confirm the front-clip harness still fits snugly and cannot ride up or let Kibo back out. Keep his ID collar on, but don’t improvise a second leash attachment unless the equipment is designed for it.
- Hold a folded section of the longer leash close to the harness to create a short working length, while keeping the remaining leash neatly gathered. Keep slack off the ground.
- Use two hands as needed, but never wrap the leash around your hand, wrist, waist, or body, and don’t tie knots or make a makeshift shortening loop.
- At Prospect Park entrances, slow down before reaching the curb, scan for bikes and scooters, step to the side or turn around when traffic approaches, and keep Kibo on the side away from the path. If the entrance is too crowded to manage the longer leash closely, take a quieter side-street route or make only a brief potty trip until the replacement arrives.

The prior “short leash near entrances” rule is subordinate to equipment integrity: an intact, well-managed longer leash is preferable to a damaged shorter one.

The available records contain the 2027 terms, not the 2028 premiums or employer-deposit schedule. So this is a baseline comparison only; it does not make a 2028 election.

2027 baseline, using 26 biweekly paychecks:

                         HDHP                 PPO
Employee premium        $98/paycheck          $164/paycheck
Annual employee premium $2,548                $4,264
Deductible              $2,300                $750
Coinsurance             10% after deductible  20% after deductible
Employer HSA            $900                  $0
HSA eligible            Yes                   No

The HDHP premium is $66 lower per paycheck and $1,716 lower annually:

$4,264 − $2,548 = $1,716

If the full $900 employer HSA contribution is available and usable, the HDHP’s accounting advantage becomes $2,616:

$1,716 premium savings + $900 employer HSA = $2,616

That $900 should not be treated as an employee-premium reduction, however. It is separate employer funding, and it does not necessarily arrive when medical bills are due.

Practical tradeoffs

HDHP advantages:

- Much lower fixed payroll premium.
- $900 of employer HSA funding.
- HSA eligibility and potential tax-advantaged savings.
- Lower post-deductible coinsurance rate: 10% rather than 20%.
- For low or moderate use, the premium savings and employer funding create a substantial cushion.

HDHP risks:

- You may face the full $2,300 deductible before the plan begins sharing most nonpreventive costs.
- A large bill early in the year can arrive before enough HSA money has accumulated.
- The employer HSA contribution does not eliminate the need for personal liquidity.
- The out-of-pocket maximum is not in the available terms, so the worst-case comparison is incomplete.

PPO advantages:

- Much lower deductible: $750 versus $2,300.
- More predictable early-year costs and less need to front a large medical bill.
- Better fit if you expect substantial care, have limited cash reserves, or place a high value on predictable cost sharing.

PPO risks:

- $1,716 more in annual premiums before considering any medical spending.
- No employer HSA contribution and no HSA eligibility.
- Its 20% coinsurance after the deductible is higher than the HDHP’s 10%.
- The extra premium may buy more predictable cash flow without necessarily producing lower total annual cost.

Effect of the unstated HSA schedule

The schedule matters primarily for liquidity, not for the eventual annual accounting total.

The known 2027 pattern was four $225 deposits in January, April, July, and October. If 2028 used the same pattern, cumulative employer funding would be approximately:

- After January: $225
- After April: $450
- After July: $675
- After October: $900

Under that schedule, the HDHP is economically attractive over the full year, but early-year medical bills may still need to be paid from cash or employee HSA contributions. A front-loaded $900 deposit would improve the HDHP’s early-year risk; a back-loaded schedule would worsen it. If deposits depend on continued employment, eligibility, or other conditions, the $900 should also be treated as contingent until those terms are confirmed.

The right comparison when the 2028 materials arrive is therefore:

1. Annual employee premiums.
2. Deductible and out-of-pocket maximum.
3. Expected routine-care costs.
4. Employer HSA amount and exact deposit dates.
5. Whether the HSA funding is available before likely bills.
6. Network, prescription, laboratory, and facility-cost differences.

For now, the last posted terms favor the HDHP on expected annual cost, while the PPO mainly provides protection against early-year cash-flow strain and a lower deductible. The 2028 conclusion should remain open until the new premiums, out-of-pocket maximums, and HSA schedule are stated.

input.title: Sphere 2027 Individual HDHP and PPO — Archive Comparison
input.body:
Sphere 2027 Individual Medical Plans
Archive comparison date: January 1, 2028
Coverage year: January 1–December 31, 2027

Purpose
Neutral archival record of the posted 2027 individual HDHP and PPO terms and the associated open-enrollment deadline. This document records plan features without recommending either plan.

Plan comparison

| Term | Individual HDHP | Individual PPO |
|---|---:|---:|
| Employee premium | $98 per biweekly paycheck | $164 per biweekly paycheck |
| Annual employee premium (26 paychecks) | $2,548 | $4,264 |
| Deductible | $2,300 | $750 |
| Coinsurance after deductible | 10% | 20% |
| Preventive care | Fully covered | Fully covered |
| HSA eligibility | Eligible | Not eligible |
| Employer HSA funding | $900 annually, through four $225 deposits in January, April, July, and October | None |

Annual premium difference

The HDHP payroll premium was $1,716 lower annually than the PPO premium, based on 26 biweekly paychecks ($4,264 − $2,548). Employer HSA funding was separate from the medical-plan premium and was not a premium reduction.

Enrollment timing

- Open enrollment opened Monday, October 5, 2026.
- Enrollment deadline: Friday, October 23, 2026 at 5:00 PM Eastern.
- Elections submitted during the window were effective for the 2027 plan year.
- Sphere’s FAQ stated that medical-plan elections generally could not be changed after the deadline without a qualifying life event.

Archive notes

- The posted 2027 comparison records no out-of-pocket maximum for either plan; no value is added here.
- No routine-visit copays, prescription terms, network details, or other cost-sharing provisions are included because they were not part of the archived 2027 terms summarized here.
- The archive is a factual comparison, not a new election or a recommendation.

input.body: Request changes: please do not add a second, side-by-side canary-response procedure. `rb_metrics_router_canary` is the accepted current reference and already defines the owner-led-window thresholds, stop/recovery flow, rollback conditions, fresh opening decision, and rejoin boundaries. input.body:
Not implementation-ready; please keep this blocked and correct the handoff record.

The release-candidate manifest is authoritative and requires ios-package, android-package, web-package, and desktop-package. The current handoff omits desktop-package, and the primary-platform guidance cannot waive a manifest-listed required output.

There are also two metadata/version failures: android-package records canonical_package_version 8.0.7 while the handoff names 8.1.0, and web-package has no generated_artifact_metadata. The web build attestation does not replace the required per-output metadata, and same-major-line compatibility is not sufficient; each listed artifact must carry generated-artifact metadata whose canonical_package_version exactly matches the handoff record. Please add the missing required output and metadata, regenerate/replace Android from 8.1.0, rerun the complete manifest-based check, and only then set implementation_ready=true.

- This is the amount you authorize Sphere to deduct from future paychecks and deposit into an HSA.

- You need an initial employee HSA payroll amount if you want employee contributions to begin with the 2027 plan year, but the amount is not necessarily permanently locked at open enrollment.
- Sphere’s FAQ says that, if you are enrolled in the HDHP, you may change prospective per-paycheck HSA contributions during the plan year. A change affects only future payrolls; it does not retroactively change deductions that have already occurred.
- The employer’s $900 HDHP contribution is separate from your payroll election and is not something you set.

What you still need to decide by October 23

1. Which medical plan to elect: HDHP or PPO.
2. If selecting the HDHP, what initial employee HSA payroll contribution amount—if any—you want to start.
3. If selecting the HDHP, how much total HSA funding you want to target, taking into account the separate $900 employer contribution and the amount you would contribute yourself.
4. Whether the initial HSA amount fits your paycheck budget and can be changed later if your circumstances change.

In short: the medical-plan choice is the decision you must treat as final by the deadline. The initial HSA payroll amount is also part of the enrollment setup, but its practical commitment is more flexible because future contributions can be adjusted prospectively during the year. results.content:
I’m missing the exact three-option quote in the available history, so I can’t responsibly compare their prices or terms line by line. Assuming the choices are:

1. Warranty replacement cylinder
2. Paid cylinder repair/replacement
3. Replace the chair

Practical comparison:

- Warranty cylinder: Best value if the chair frame, five-star base, casters, seat mechanism, and upholstery are otherwise sound. It avoids paying for a problem the manufacturer has accepted and preserves the chair you already fit-tested.
- Paid cylinder: Reasonable only if the warranty excludes the cylinder, labor, or shipping and the chair is otherwise worth keeping. Get the exact compatible cylinder and installed cost first; “universal” fit alone is not enough.
- New chair: Best if the chair also has a cracked or distorted base, persistent wobble, damaged mechanism, worn casters, major upholstery failure, unclear repair history, or multiple chairs are aging at once. It is the cleanest option but usually the least economical if the cylinder is the only fault.

Recommendation: choose the warranty cylinder, provided the written warranty confirms the correct model-compatible part and gives a clear replacement or installation path. It is reasonable—not a shortcut—when the cylinder is the isolated failure. I would not pay for a cylinder or buy a whole chair yet unless the warranty process is unusually slow, excludes the needed labor, or inspection finds damage beyond the cylinder.

While waiting:

- Do not use a chair that sinks, drops suddenly, hisses, wobbles excessively, tips, has a cracked base, or shows a dent, deep corrosion, bend, or other damage around the cylinder.
- Use only a chair that holds its height and remains stable. Sit centered, keep all casters on the floor, and avoid leaning hard, rocking, standing on the seat, or using it as a step.
- Do not improvise a pipe, clamp, shim, strap, or fixed-height block around the cylinder. Lowering the chair does not make a visibly damaged or unstable cylinder safe.
- Keep the questionable chair away from Kibo and anyone else, and label it “do not use.”
- Do not drill, cut, heat, puncture, open, or hammer the gas cylinder. It is a sealed pressurized component.
- If the replacement is shipped, confirm the model and compatibility before installation. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions or use an authorized repairer; do not assume a physically fitting cylinder is safe.
- After repair, test it unoccupied first, then cycle the height adjustment, check that it holds position, and inspect for wobble or abnormal noise before resuming normal use.

For the exact recommendation between the three, send the option names, total prices, warranty coverage, and turnaround times.

Hi — I enjoyed the conversation last week. I wrote a few thoughts on how I would approach ownership for a design-system pattern after v1 ships.

The short version is that I think ownership means making the pattern easy to use correctly, not controlling every use of it. For the dashboard/onboarding work I did, the first version was useful but still too dependent on me remembering why certain choices were made. After launch I would want to document the stable parts of the pattern: which pieces should stay consistent, which pieces can flex by product context, what the empty/loading/error/permission states are, and what kind of request should cause us to revisit the pattern instead of adding one-off variants.

I would also set a light review loop with the teams using the pattern. In my agency work this sometimes got messy because clients and account teams wanted bespoke views, and I was probably too worried about saying no. I learned that it helps to have criteria written down before requests come in. If a new product team needs a variation, the question is whether the variation teaches us something reusable or whether it should stay local.

I don't think the owner has to be the person who says yes or no to everything. I think the owner should keep the pattern understandable, make tradeoffs visible, and notice when the pattern is becoming either too rigid or too vague. That's the kind of systems ownership I am interested in doing more of.

entries.title: shard-keeper: rollback procedure (post-Apr-18 hardened path)
entries.body:
1. Remove the affected replica from follower reads.
2. Verify that the lease holder and epoch remain stable, with no acquisition or relinquishment events, stale-owner messages, overlapping leadership, or write errors.
3. Confirm that the replica is making forward catch-up progress.
4. Re-enter the follower read pool only after disk latency is back at baseline and lag is below one second for fifteen continuous minutes.
5. Restart only if the replica stops progressing after the lease-safety checks. Do not use an automatic timer response as the restart condition.

entries.title: shard-keeper: verify lease convergence after failover
entries.body:
Process readiness alone is not the exit condition. In the staging failover drill, all replacement replicas reported ready after 18 seconds, but lease ownership did not converge until 96 seconds. Before declaring the failover complete, verify all of the following: 1. Every partition has exactly one owner. 2. Lease epochs remain monotonic. 3. No stale-owner messages appear for two full lease-renewal intervals. If any of those checks fail, keep the failover open and page the shard-keeper owner. Renewal-warning versus lease transfer: `renewal deadline exceeded` alone does not prove a lease transfer. Check for a changed lease epoch, explicit acquisition or relinquishment, overlapping leadership, and post-event replication convergence. If the holder and epoch remain unchanged, no overlap occurs, and lag returns to baseline, treat the event as a delayed renewal rather than a failover; do not automatically restart.

## Production lease-loss serving-gate invariant

On lease-loss notification, close the old holder's serving gate before it can return another routing response. The periodic poll is only a backup detector, not the serving-safety mechanism. Production verification must include:
- gate closure before any later routing response
- exactly one serving holder throughout the transfer
- lease-loss notification to gate-close latency
- stale routing responses
- replacement acquisition time
- request p99
- errors
- restarts

A slow handoff or convergence warning is an availability signal to investigate separately. By itself, it is not evidence that the old holder served after lease loss or that the serving-safety invariant failed. The owner map and mapped deployment responsibility remain unchanged.

1. Systems-level technical scope

I have been working across service boundaries to define invariants, review failure modes, and make escalation paths explicit—not just implementing within one service. For example, the `shard_region` → `storage_region` change passed cardinality and alert-source checks but failed the cross-service parity fixture because `rollup-service` still read the old key. That exposed a producer-consumer contract failure before production and led to a required executable parity gate for covered label renames. I also clarified the cross-service acknowledgement contract so each service defines its own durability boundary, retryable failures, and supported retry horizon.

2. Enabling other engineers through durable mechanisms

The work has been converted into reusable controls rather than depending on my personal review: executable parity fixtures, label-cardinality preflight, alert-source classification, and owner sign-off for affected services. In Lantern, ordinary qualifying room admissions moved to Iris under explicit service-area, purpose, provenance, and permission criteria, while I retained only contract, failure-mode, and provenance exceptions. Similarly, the importer now reauthorizes before each fetch and publication and invalidates partial imports on denial, turning a permission concern into a durable fail-closed mechanism.

3. Explicit ownership boundaries

My responsibility is to define and review cross-service invariants, failure modes, ownership seams, and escalation boundaries. The mapped service owners retain implementation, telemetry, operational readiness, and release decisions: I remain primary for `metrics-router`, `ingest-edge`, and `shard-keeper`, with Wes, Yuki, and the Cyrus team as the respective backups; Cyrus’s team owns `rollup-service`, and Nadia owns alerting/dashboards. Wes’s practical first-pass scope covers `metrics-router` canaries and `ingest-edge` staging through the deploy pipeline, but does not change the owner map or extend to solo `shard-keeper` work.

input.title: Historical kickoff note — May 8, 2023 runbook-ownership audit
input.body:
Historical kickoff note

Date: May 8, 2023
Audit lead: Hema
Status at kickoff: Starting

Purpose
Conduct the required May runbook-ownership audit after the April 18 outage review. Establish explicit primary and backup ownership for every service, eliminate fuzzy ownership boundaries, and leave a durable record for operations and escalation.

Scope and working method
- Review every service using one ownership one-pager per service.
- Record a primary owner and a backup for each service.
- Start with Alex’s primary-owner list: `metrics-router`, `ingest-edge`, and `shard-keeper`.
- Use a separate touch/dependency list to identify services that interact with those systems without turning every dependency into an ownership dispute.
- Treat `legacy-aggregator`, `rollup-service`, and other historical consumers as explicit edge cases rather than silently assigning practical ownership.
- Nadia cross-reviews the service areas she touches.
- Wes is being folded into the review ahead of joining the rotation in two weeks.

Known risk entering the audit
The `shard-keeper` runbook was the worst item in the set: approximately 18 months stale and missing the newer label-routing material. It was expected to require the most substantive rewrite. The `shard-keeper` migration remains paused pending completion of the ownership audit.

Kickoff assignments
- Hema: run the audit and keep the pass mechanical and explicit.
- Alex: cover `metrics-router`, `ingest-edge`, and `shard-keeper`; bring the primary-owner and touch/dependency lists.
- Nadia: cross-review the service areas she touches.
- Wes: participate as part of rotation onboarding and review preparation.

Completion criteria
1. Every in-scope service has a named primary and backup.
2. Ownership, backup coverage, and escalation boundaries are written down rather than inferred from history or informal practice.
3. The `shard-keeper` runbook is brought current, including the newer label-routing material.
4. Historical or ambiguously owned services are called out explicitly for resolution.
5. The owner map is ready for the scheduled May 22 audit review.

Historical follow-through
The audit was later reported complete with the owner map locked on May 22. The resulting map assigned Alex as primary for `metrics-router`, `ingest-edge`, and `shard-keeper`; Wes backed up `metrics-router`, Yuki backed up `ingest-edge`, Cyrus’s team backed up `shard-keeper`, Nadia owned alerting/dashboards, and Cyrus’s team owned `rollup-service`. The final `shard-keeper` documentation also required a pre-push sync with the other owner or the on-call.

Source basis
Reconstructed from the May 2–8, 2023 audit planning and kickoff records, the April 28 incident-review rules, the May 11 progress check, and the May 22 audit closeout record. This note preserves the historical distinction between kickoff intent, known risks, and later outcomes.

## Pilot prevention note — Nov 14, 2023

The first concrete prevention case for this first-cut checklist came from a rollup-service validation metrics proposal.

Proposed shape that did not ship:
`rollup_validation_sample_total{validation_result="match|mismatch", replay_source_id="$source_id"}`

Why it failed the checklist:
- `replay_source_id` is a raw replay-stream identifier.
- Cyrus's sample showed the value is effectively unbounded across replay sources, jobs, chunks, and backfills.
- The debugging need was real, but the raw identifier belongs in logs rather than as a metrics label.

Accepted shape:
- Keep raw `replay_source_id` in logs for debugging.
- Use a bounded `source_class` metric label for rollup-service validation dashboards.
- Preserve validation visibility without introducing an unbounded label into the metrics pipeline.

This is evidence that the first-cut Cardinality Guardrails review can prevent a bad label shape without blocking the debugging need. It does not make Cardinality Guardrails mature, complete, or a general telemetry rewrite.

excerpts:
Goal: first-cut controls for the Q4 Cardinality Guardrails work; keep it tied to the September mirror/replay legacy-aggregator wobble without turning validation movement into rollback criteria.
Rows to include:
1. Label limits: failure mode is unbounded or newly introduced label keys/values causing fanout; candidate control is a narrow allowlist or budget per sensitive label family; preflight should flag new high-cardinality labels before a metrics-router or shard-keeper push.
2. Alert-source semantics: failure mode is responders treating replay/mirror validation movement as live-path rollback evidence; candidate control is dashboard and alert wording that marks live metrics-router traffic separately from replay or mirror validation samples.
3. Label-change preflight: failure mode is a config or parser change adding labels without checking cardinality behavior; candidate control is a pre-push checklist with sample counts, source label, owner, and rollback/non-rollback semantics.
Non-goals: no customer-facing dashboard, no general telemetry rewrite, no legacy-aggregator retirement claim, no claim that the 2% replay sample creates immediate storage savings, no Q3 incident framing.
Monday questions: what cost examples can Cyrus bring by label family; which preflight checks are service-owned by Alex versus data-platform advisory; what would make the first cut too broad.

input.title: Cardinality Guardrails — first prevention result
input.body:
# Cardinality Guardrails: first prevention result

## Onboarding case study

Cardinality Guardrails began as a narrow, first-cut review for label changes—not a general telemetry rewrite. Its first concrete prevention result came from a rollup-service validation-metrics proposal.

The proposed metric was:

`rollup_validation_sample_total{validation_result="match|mismatch", replay_source_id="$source_id"}`

The review identified `replay_source_id` as an effectively unbounded raw replay-stream identifier across sources, jobs, chunks, and backfills. Shipping it as a metric label could have created uncontrolled series growth, even though the debugging need was legitimate.

The team kept the raw identifier in logs and replaced it with a bounded `source_class` metric label for dashboards. That preserved validation visibility while preventing a risky label shape before it shipped.

The takeaway for onboarding is simple: use the preflight to challenge the label shape, not the underlying debugging goal. This was evidence that the first-cut practice could prevent a concrete issue; it was not evidence that Cardinality Guardrails was mature or complete.

input.title: Cardinality Guardrails — original first-release historical scope
input.body:
Historical scope note — original first release (October 2023)

Cardinality Guardrails began as a narrow Q4 control slice responding to the September mirror/replay cardinality wobble—not as a mature telemetry-governance program. The initial release covered three controls for label changes affecting metrics-router, shard-keeper, and, where applicable, rollup-service: label-cardinality limits/preflight, alert-source classification, and cross-service parity for changed label names or semantics.

The preflight required an owner, source, expected boundedness, and representative cardinality evidence; live-path evidence was required for live labels, while replay or mirror data remained investigation/validation evidence rather than rollback criteria. Cost and fanout analysis was directional and advisory, with implementation, enforcement, release, and rollback remaining with the mapped service owners.

Explicit non-goals were a general telemetry rewrite, a customer-facing dashboard, legacy-aggregator retirement, centralized enforcement ownership, and any claim that the initial slice delivered immediate storage savings. The first release was intentionally first-cut: concrete and reviewable, but not complete or organization-wide governance.

input.body:
Request changes: the implementation does not match the standing customer-visible chronology policy for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce.

- Visible order must be controlled only by the authoritative `source_timestamp`, not `processed_at`. The current `records.sort((a, b) => b.processed_at.localeCompare(a.processed_at))` would let processing time reorder the explanation; the delayed-retry fixture exposes that defect.

They may be retained/displayed as operational/audit fields, but must never determine customer-visible order. (The policy also treats observation, serialization, processing, render, and retry times as non-ordering audit metadata; do not substitute any of them for source time.)

- Keep chronology claims narrow: it may state the sequence/order represented by authoritative source times. It must not imply causation, release readiness/approval, employee performance, ownership or authority transfer, or any authorization/expansion decision. It must not present processing, arrival/observation, serialization, render, or retry timing as event chronology.

Please update the implementation and regressions for delayed/retried records, missing/malformed source timestamps, and equal source timestamps, then rerun the relevant tests.

Alex

input.title: Secondary-page deadline and Wes’s June 21 example
input.body:
Secondary-page deadline

If the primary is still engaged or the issue is not isolated, page or explicitly pull in the secondary within 45 minutes of the incident clock starting. Measure the deadline by the timestamp of the page or explicit pull-in, not by the secondary’s acknowledgment or join time. The engagement must occur before 45:00; a later acknowledgment does not invalidate a timely page, and acknowledgment alone does not prove that the page was timely.

Example: Wes’s first solo on-call shift overnight on June 21 included a minor metrics-router cardinality blip. At the 40-minute mark, while he was not fully sure of the diagnosis, he pulled Alex in as secondary. Wes then got the issue sorted; no further escalation was needed. This is a timely secondary engagement because the explicit pull-in occurred at minute 40, before the 45-minute deadline.

results.content:
Lantern v0 failure-modes note
Current internal v0 only

Purpose

This note describes how Lantern can fail or appear incomplete during the limited internal v0 period. It is a usage boundary, not a postmortem or roadmap. v0 covers backend-emitted deploy movement, provenance-backed ownership changes, and permission-safe incident-load summaries.

Alex — data and failure-mode ownership

1. Stale deploy movement

Failure mode:
The deploy feed is delayed, incomplete, or reflects an older backend state.

Expected behavior:
Lantern must render only deploy states actually emitted by the source system. It must preserve the distinction between observed time and collection time where available.

Boundary:
The surface must not manufacture intermediate transitions, infer that a deployment completed, or present stale movement as current. If freshness or state is unavailable, the data should remain absent or explicitly unknown rather than guessed.

2. Missing provenance

Failure mode:
An ownership record may be true in the authoritative owner map but lack recorded provenance that Lantern can present and rely on.

Expected behavior:
The ownership card does not render.

Boundary:
Lantern must not infer ownership from surrounding context, activity, code movement, or a human’s prior knowledge. A sparse ownership section is intentional provenance discipline, not evidence that the underlying owner map is wrong or incomplete.

3. Permission-limited incident summaries

Failure mode:
A viewer does not have permission to see the incident-load data needed for a summary, or the available projection is not allowed for that audience.

Expected behavior:
The incident-load summary is omitted or limited to the permitted projection.

Boundary:
Lantern must not expose raw incident bodies, responder details, unpermissioned status chatter, or hidden source-system information. The UI should not fill the gap by implying incident state that the backend did not emit.

4. Non-comprehensive surface

Failure mode:
Viewers interpret the visible cards and summaries as a complete account of deploys, ownership, or incident activity.

Expected behavior:
The surface should be understood as a filtered view of provenanced, permission-safe facts available to the current viewer.

Boundary:
Absence of a card does not establish that the underlying event, owner, or incident does not exist. During v0, missing data, missing provenance, permission filtering, and intentionally excluded signal types can all produce an incomplete-looking surface.

Iris — UI interpretation ownership

- Make the displayed state and omissions legible without implying certainty beyond the data.
- Do not infer transitions, causality, ownership, or incident details from gaps in the backend-emitted record.
- Distinguish “not shown in this viewer/v0 surface” from “does not exist.”
- Explain sparse ownership results as recorded-provenance behavior, not as an ownership dispute or product failure.
- Keep labels and summaries bounded to the permission-safe projection; do not expose raw operational detail.
- Preserve the v0 framing: Lantern is showing selected, trustworthy system movement—not a comprehensive operational or status dashboard.

Decision: Lantern v0 scope and contract

Lantern v0 will expose three signal families:

- Deploy movement
- Ownership changes
- Normalized incident load

Product-facing views will consume an allowlisted summary projection. Raw incident/page payloads, responder details, and source-system links are out of scope because they are too noisy and may cross audience boundaries.

The v0 event contract must make provenance and permissions explicit before the product surface is considered shippable. Provenance must identify the originating source and emitting adapter; the projection boundary must prevent unauthorized or overly detailed operational data from reaching product-facing readers.

The UI will render only states emitted by the backend. It must not infer state transitions or invent semantics for missing signals.

Deferred from v0:

- Query-volume deltas
- Code-movement inference
- Raw incident/page payloads

This keeps the first cut visibly useful while preserving trustworthy event semantics and clear access boundaries.

sources.label: Assistant's reply to Alex Valdez, message 001293
excerpts:
Design-review decision: keep admission rejection; do not evict already queued requests.

With a hard 20,000-request cap, the queue is also a commitment boundary: once metrics-router admits work, it must either process it, retry it under an explicit policy, or report its failure. Evicting the oldest item after admission silently discards accepted work, breaks FIFO expectations, complicates client retry behavior, and can create loss or duplicate-processing ambiguity. The freshness improvement in Wes’s load test is not sufficient justification for changing delivery semantics.

Continue to reject before admission:

- At the cap, return HTTP 429.
- Do not mutate the queue for the rejected request.
- Include the established retry signal, preferably `Retry-After` or an equivalent bounded backoff hint.
- Resume admission as soon as capacity is actually available.
- Count rejected requests separately from accepted, completed, failed, and dropped work.
- Do not introduce an eviction counter with a nonzero value; for this policy, eviction should remain zero.

If freshness is a product requirement, implement it later as an explicitly named policy—such as lossy sampling, coalescing, or a caller-selected “drop-oldest” mode—with separate semantics and metrics. It should not be hidden inside the normal bounded queue.

Focused tests

1. Retry signaling

- Fill the queue to exactly 20,000 items; verify the next request receives 429.
- Verify a full-queue rejection does not increase queue depth, accepted count, in-flight count, or completion work.
- Verify the response contains a valid retry signal with the documented units and bounds.
- Verify clients retrying after the signal are admitted once capacity is available.
- Verify repeated retries while the queue remains full continue to receive 429 without creating server-side retry state or a retry storm.
- Test the boundary at 19,999, 20,000, and 20,001 attempted admissions.
- Under concurrent producers, verify no request is reported accepted unless it has a reserved queue slot.

2. Ordering

- Admit uniquely numbered requests, fill the queue, drain it, and verify admitted requests are processed in FIFO order.
- Verify the request rejected at the cap never appears in the queue or completion stream unless it is later explicitly retried and admitted.
- Verify a retry is ordered according to its later admission, not its original rejected attempt.
- Race producers and the consumer at the cap boundary; verify the implementation has one unambiguous linearization point for dequeue versus admission.
- Verify rejected requests cannot overtake already admitted requests.
- Verify queue ordering remains intact through a consumer pause, resume, and normal drain.

3. Accounting and invariants

Assert continuously, including under concurrency:

- `queued <= 20,000`.
- `accepted = queued + in_flight + completed + terminal_failed` according to the service’s precise lifecycle definition.
- `rejected_429` counts requests refused before admission.
- `evicted = 0`.
- `dropped_accepted_work = 0`.
- Every accepted request has exactly one terminal outcome.
- No rejected request is acknowledged as accepted or counted as completed.
- No request is counted twice when dequeue, processing failure, retry, and acknowledgement happen concurrently.
- Queue depth, oldest age, accepted count, rejected count, completion count, and failure count agree with an independent test-harness ledger.
- Memory and queue-byte limits, if separate from item count, cannot be bypassed by admitting oversized requests.

Include fault-injection cases for a producer racing with a consumer, consumer cancellation after dequeue, process restart, and acknowledgement failure. These are where an eviction-style implementation commonly turns into silent loss or duplication.

4. Recovery after the queue falls below the cap

- Fill the queue, confirm 429s, consume one item, and verify the next eligible request is admitted promptly.
- Consume several items and verify admission resumes one-for-one with released capacity.
- Drain the queue to zero; verify producers do not remain stuck in a “full” state.
- Apply sustained input above consumer capacity, then reduce input below consumer capacity; verify queue depth and age fall and admission recovers without manual intervention.
- Repeat full/relieved cycles and verify no capacity leak, stale-full flag, deadlock, or monotonic counter corruption.
- Pause and resume the consumer while producers continue; verify full-queue rejection during the pause and normal admission after resume.
- Inject processing failures and retries; verify recovery does not exceed the cap or reorder already admitted work.
- Restart the router at full and partially drained states, according to the durability contract, and verify queued work is either recovered or explicitly reported as failed—never silently discarded.
- Verify alerting and dashboards distinguish temporary 429 backpressure from accepted-work loss.

The acceptance criterion should be: at most 20,000 queued requests, no silent loss of admitted work, FIFO ordering for admitted requests, accurate lifecycle accounting, and automatic admission recovery once capacity is released.

sources.label: Assistant's reply to Alex Valdez, message 001293
excerpts:
Design-review decision: keep admission rejection; do not evict already queued requests.

With a hard 20,000-request cap, the queue is also a commitment boundary: once metrics-router admits work, it must either process it, retry it under an explicit policy, or report its failure. Evicting the oldest item after admission silently discards accepted work, breaks FIFO expectations, complicates client retry behavior, and can create loss or duplicate-processing ambiguity. The freshness improvement in Wes’s load test is not sufficient justification for changing delivery semantics.

Continue to reject before admission:

- At the cap, return HTTP 429.
- Do not mutate the queue for the rejected request.
- Include the established retry signal, preferably `Retry-After` or an equivalent bounded backoff hint.
- Resume admission as soon as capacity is actually available.
- Count rejected requests separately from accepted, completed, failed, and dropped work.
- Do not introduce an eviction counter with a nonzero value; for this policy, eviction should remain zero.

If freshness is a product requirement, implement it later as an explicitly named policy—such as lossy sampling, coalescing, or a caller-selected “drop-oldest” mode—with separate semantics and metrics. It should not be hidden inside the normal bounded queue.

Focused tests

1. Retry signaling

- Fill the queue to exactly 20,000 items; verify the next request receives 429.
- Verify a full-queue rejection does not increase queue depth, accepted count, in-flight count, or completion work.
- Verify the response contains a valid retry signal with the documented units and bounds.
- Verify clients retrying after the signal are admitted once capacity is available.
- Verify repeated retries while the queue remains full continue to receive 429 without creating server-side retry state or a retry storm.
- Test the boundary at 19,999, 20,000, and 20,001 attempted admissions.
- Under concurrent producers, verify no request is reported accepted unless it has a reserved queue slot.

2. Ordering

- Admit uniquely numbered requests, fill the queue, drain it, and verify admitted requests are processed in FIFO order.
- Verify the request rejected at the cap never appears in the queue or completion stream unless it is later explicitly retried and admitted.
- Verify a retry is ordered according to its later admission, not its original rejected attempt.
- Race producers and the consumer at the cap boundary; verify the implementation has one unambiguous linearization point for dequeue versus admission.
- Verify rejected requests cannot overtake already admitted requests.
- Verify queue ordering remains intact through a consumer pause, resume, and normal drain.

3. Accounting and invariants

Assert continuously, including under concurrency:

- `queued <= 20,000`.
- `accepted = queued + in_flight + completed + terminal_failed` according to the service’s precise lifecycle definition.
- `rejected_429` counts requests refused before admission.
- `evicted = 0`.
- `dropped_accepted_work = 0`.
- Every accepted request has exactly one terminal outcome.
- No rejected request is acknowledged as accepted or counted as completed.

input.title: Bounded queue and retryable backpressure rollout: stop conditions
input.body:
Purpose

This entry is the authoritative stop checklist for the tenant-bounded queue and retryable pre-acceptance backpressure rollout. Stop the current stage immediately, hold further movement, and enter the rollback/recovery path whenever any condition below occurs. A stop is not cleared by a later recovery; resume requires the applicable fresh decision and fully observed recovery evidence.

Rollout limits and invariants

- Global queue capacity is hard-capped at 2,048 batches. Never exceed the cap.
- Pending work is capped at 64 batches per tenant. Additional work must be refused through the retryable backpressure path before acceptance; a tenant must not exceed the limit.
- Retryable queue-full responses are pre-acceptance refusals, not accepted work and not evidence that the tenant cap was exceeded.
- Any eviction of already accepted or queued work is a stop condition. The bounded-queue policy rejects before admission; it does not drop or evict admitted work.
- Any accepted-batch loss, dropped accepted work, silent discard, or unaccounted accepted batch is a stop condition.
- Every accepted batch must reconcile to exactly one terminal result. Stop on a missing, duplicate, or otherwise inconsistent terminal outcome, or on any lifecycle-accounting mismatch.
- Stop if queue depth, memory/queue-byte limits, or other admission accounting can bypass the configured bounds.

Hard metric stops

- Queue-wait p99 exceeds 400 ms for five consecutive minutes.
- Retryable queue-full responses exceed 0.5% for five consecutive minutes.
- Any tenant exceeds 64 pending batches, or the per-tenant bound is not enforced.
- The global queue exceeds 2,048 batches, or queue admission reports success without a reserved bounded slot.

Data-integrity and cross-service health stops

Stop on any departure from baseline in any of the following:

- Consistency checks.
- Parity checks.
- Dropped-series checks.
- Route checks or route parity.
- Shard-keeper lease health.
- Rollup-service health or parity.
- The full health set.

Also stop for any accepted-batch loss, unexpected loss, duplicate processing, missing terminal result, reconciliation failure, or evidence that an acknowledgement, restart, cancellation, processing failure, or retry can silently lose or duplicate accepted work.

Backpressure and failure-signal stops

- The retryable backpressure or queue-full counter disappears, becomes unavailable, or changes unexpectedly.
- Full-queue refusals are not generated before acceptance, do not remain separately observable from accepted work, or do not carry the established retry signal (Retry-After or an equivalent bounded backoff hint).
- Repeated or worsening timeout bursts or error bursts return.
- Retry behavior creates a retry storm, server-side retry state for pre-admission refusals, stale-full state, deadlock, capacity leak, or failure to resume admission promptly once capacity is released.
- Dashboards or alerts cannot distinguish temporary pre-acceptance 429/backpressure from loss of accepted work.

Instance, rollout, and recovery stops

- Any instance exceeds its defined resource budget.
- Any instance terminates or restarts unexpectedly during the stage.
- Any replacement or new instance becomes routable before readiness and current-generation/full-health gates are satisfied.
- Active-generation consistency fails, route snapshots diverge, reload fails, or a host-local fault produces negative route-snapshot age or other invalid generation evidence.
- Retired generations accumulate above four.
- A cleanup pause exceeds 100 ms. This threshold is explicit: exceeding it stops the window immediately.
- Consumer cancellation after dequeue, acknowledgement failure, process restart, or a full/partially drained restart state leaves queued work neither recovered nor explicitly reported failed.

Response

1. Stop further rollout movement immediately; do not advance to the next stage or reopen a multi-stage window.
2. Preserve queue, tenant, admission/refusal, terminal-outcome, generation, heap, route, and cross-service health evidence.
3. Isolate or replace the affected instance through the deploy pipeline when the fault is host-local; do not use a configuration rollback as a substitute for host-local remediation.
4. Roll back or recover according to the applicable existing metrics-router procedure for data-integrity, route, generation, or cross-service failures.
5. After recovery, verify the full health set and all bounded-queue invariants at baseline. A fresh applicable decision authorizes exactly one fully observed recovery push; it does not authorize reopening a multi-push window.

Normal full-queue behavior is not itself a stop: reject new work before admission with HTTP 429 and the established retry signal, leave the queue unchanged, count the refusal separately, and resume admission as soon as capacity is actually available. The acceptance standard remains: bounds hold, no accepted work is silently lost or duplicated, admitted work retains its required ordering, lifecycle accounting is exact, and admission recovers automatically after capacity is released.

input.body:
Hema quarterly Infra onboarding facilitator sheet
Date: 2028-01-01
Module: Quarterly infra-rotation onboarding: timed scenarios
Format: tabletop practice only; not a production runbook, production window, deployment authorization, standing approval gate, or ownership change.

Purpose
Evaluate whether participants keep routing, terminal accounting, rollback evidence, and ownership boundaries explicit under the three adopted incident-practice scenarios. Participants must address all three scenarios explicitly.

Roles
- Wes: teaches the responder path.
- Nadia: reviews postmortem framing and control analysis.
- Alex: maintains only the bounded cross-service failure cases and the named failure-mode boundary; do not assign implementation, release, or rollback ownership to Alex because he is facilitating a case.
- Mapped service owner: retains implementation, release, and rollback decisions.

Facilitation flow
1. State the tabletop-only boundary and read one scenario at a time.
2. Ask for the participant’s decision, evidence, owner, and stop condition.
3. Score only observable statements or artifacts; do not award credit for intent, restart activity, or an unverified inference.
4. If a boundary is missed, record the miss and use the remaining time for one targeted rerun; do not convert the exercise into a live action.
5. Debrief on evidence, ownership, and the failure-mode boundary.

Scenario 1 — Over-budget replacement remains unroutable
Prompt
A replacement instance exceeds the fixed readiness budget. The participant must decide whether it may receive traffic and what evidence would change that decision.

Expected response
- Keep the replacement unroutable after the readiness budget is missed.
- Do not treat restart, retry, or elapsed time as acceptance/readiness evidence.
- Name the missing readiness evidence and the bounded next observation required in the tabletop.
- Preserve the mapped owner’s implementation, release, and rollback authority.

Pass
- Explicitly says “over budget” does not make the instance routable.
- Rejects restart as acceptance evidence.
- Records the readiness gap and keeps the decision within the exercise boundary.

Fail
- Routes the instance because it restarted, responded once, or appears healthy without the required readiness evidence.
- Uses the tabletop answer as permission for a production change.

Scenario 2 — Cancellation race after acceptance
Prompt
An action has already been accepted. Cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and result publication race with one another. Ask how the participant preserves identity and accounting.

Expected response
- Preserve exactly one durable attempt_id for the accepted action.
- Produce exactly one terminal result, even if cancellation, disconnect, or recovery also occurs.
- Make the one winning terminal path drive both the caller-visible result and exactly one matching accounting contribution.
- Distinguish cancellation from caller disconnect and process recovery; do not collapse them into an unqualified failure.
- Keep implementation, release, and rollback with the mapped owner; keep a triggered reviewer confined to the named failure-mode boundary.

Pass
- States the durable attempt identity and the single-terminal-result invariant.
- Reconciles the caller result and accounting contribution to the same winning path.
- Identifies the event classification and preserves ownership boundaries.

Fail
- Creates a second attempt identity, publishes two terminal results, or counts both competing paths.
- Lets caller disconnect erase the accepted action or treats process restart as a new accepted action.
- Assigns the reviewer or facilitator implementation, release, or rollback authority.

Scenario 3 — Replay sample is not live rollback evidence
Prompt
A replay sample appears to reproduce a failure and is offered as justification for rollback. Ask what may and may not be concluded.

Expected response
- Treat the replay as a tabletop/debugging sample, not as live rollback criteria.
- Do not infer live production state, accepted-batch status, point loss, or rollback safety from replay output alone.
- Identify the evidence still missing, including durable correlated identity or a verified live source where the scenario requires it.
- Stop at the unresolved evidence boundary; do not authorize another production window, ramp, rollback, or ownership change.

Pass
- Explicitly rejects replay samples as live rollback evidence.
- Separates observed behavior from unestablished live state and names the missing evidence.
- Preserves the mapped owner’s implementation and rollback decisions.

Fail
- Uses replay output alone to trigger rollback, declare a live incident, or claim accepted work was lost or completed.
- Treats an uncorrelated sample as proof of live eligibility or safety.

Scoring record
Participant/group: ____________________    Facilitator: ____________________

Scenario 1:   Pass / Fail    Evidence or quote: ______________________________
Scenario 2:   Pass / Fail    Evidence or quote: ______________________________
Scenario 3:   Pass / Fail    Evidence or quote: ______________________________

Critical boundary misses:
- Routed an over-budget replacement without readiness evidence:  Yes / No
- Counted restart as acceptance evidence:  Yes / No
- Lost durable attempt identity or created more than one terminal result:  Yes / No
- Mismatched caller result and accounting contribution:  Yes / No
- Used replay as live rollback evidence:  Yes / No
- Expanded Alex/reviewer/facilitator authority beyond the named boundary:  Yes / No

Completion standard
Pass only when all three scenarios are addressed and no critical boundary miss remains unresolved. A later acknowledgment does not substitute for the required event timestamp when a timing rule is tested; record receipt latency separately. Record uncertainty explicitly rather than awarding credit for an unsupported inference.

Ownership reminder
Wes teaches responder paths. Nadia reviews postmortem framing. Alex maintains only the bounded cross-service failure cases. This sheet evaluates practice responses; it does not change service ownership or authorize production action.

Roles

Facilitation flow
1. State the tabletop-only boundary and read one scenario at a time.
2. Ask for the participant’s decision, evidence, owner, and stop condition.
3. Score only observable statements or artifacts; do not award credit for intent, restart activity, or an unverified inference.
4. If a boundary is missed, record the miss and use the remaining time for one targeted rerun; do not convert the exercise into a live action.
5. Debrief on evidence, ownership, and the failure-mode boundary.

Scenario 1 — Over-budget replacement remains unroutable
Prompt
A replacement instance exceeds the fixed readiness budget. The participant must decide whether it may receive traffic and what evidence would change that decision.

Expected response
- Keep the replacement unroutable after the readiness budget is missed.
- Do not treat restart, retry, or elapsed time as acceptance/readiness evidence.

- Preserve the mapped owner’s implementation, release, and rollback authority.

- Explicitly says “over budget” does not make the instance routable.
- Rejects restart as acceptance evidence.
- Records the readiness gap and keeps the decision within the exercise boundary.

Fail
- Routes the instance because it restarted, responded once, or appears healthy without the required readiness evidence.
- Uses the tabletop answer as permission for a production change.

Prompt

input.title: Evidence note — 2023 cross-team work with Cyrus on data-platform throughput
input.body:
2023 cross-team evidence: data-platform throughput and load-test regression work with Cyrus

Cyrus pulled me into the data-platform throughput regression in March 2023, and I agreed to investigate. On April 6, I approved Cyrus’s clean three-line PR fixing the issue he had been tracking since March/early April.

The collaboration continued in August after a load-test cardinality canary was traced to an unbounded `experiment_id` label in test traffic—not to a metrics-router deploy or router regression. I helped define a bounded, ownership-respecting rerun: notify infrastructure on-call, cap `experiment_id` to the declared set `lt-a`, `lt-b`, and `lt-c`, stop the test if the canary returned, and distinguish genuine router errors, dropped writes, or downstream lag. Cyrus reran the test on August 23; his side stopped at the planned window, the canary stayed quiet, p99 remained in the normal band, and rollup-service lag stayed flat.

Evidence of impact: I contributed cross-team diagnosis, reviewed the targeted fix, and converted an ambiguous regression/load-test failure into a safely bounded validation path without an unnecessary rollback or ownership change.

Source dates: March 9, April 6, August 16, August 21, and August 23, 2023.

Entry ID: rb_1697635080004
Title: Cardinality Guardrails: label-change preflight first cut

Body:
# Cardinality Guardrails: first control slice

This entry records the first control slice only. It does not mean Cardinality Guardrails is mature, complete, or a general telemetry rewrite.

## Controls in scope
1. Label-cardinality preflight for metrics-router and shard-keeper changes
   - Before a change ships, identify new label keys or changed value shapes.
   - Sample distinct counts for risky label families before promotion.
   - Treat `customer_id` as high-cardinality but expected; flag unbounded or one-off `experiment_id`, raw-path `route_pattern`, noisy joins with `deployment_sha`, and disallow raw `error_detail` labels.

2. Alert-source classification for replay or mirror panels
   - Dashboards and alert text must distinguish live metrics-router traffic from replay or mirror validation samples.
   - Live-path movement can start rollback discussion.
   - Replay or mirror validation movement is investigation evidence and Q4 controls input, not rollback criteria.

3. Rollup-service parity before cross-service label-name changes
   - Before label-name changes cross service boundaries, confirm rollup-service expects the same label names and semantics.
   - This is the Apr 17 failure-mode guard: shard-keeper/metrics-router label changes should not outrun the downstream rollup-service consumer.

## Non-goals
- No customer-facing dashboard.
- No legacy-aggregator retirement claim.
- No broad telemetry rewrite.
- No claim that replay or mirror movement is live rollback evidence.
- No default ownership change for enforcement; I own the service-level tradeoffs, with Cyrus advising on cost examples.

sources.label: Assistant's reply to Alex Valdez, message 001478
excerpts:
Cross-service invariant review:

Conclusion

Yes—the completion rule violated the stated lateness contract, assuming the 90-second allowance is an inclusion guarantee for records arriving after the window ends.

The window was marked complete 31 seconds after its end, but the contract allowed records to arrive for 90 seconds. That finalized the window 59 seconds too early. The latest late record arrived at 78 seconds, 12 seconds before the contractual cutoff, so it should have been included in the initial final result.

This was not an upstream or delivery-loss problem:

- Upstream accepted-point count was stable.
- Commit latency was normal.
- No route-delivery loss was observed.
- The 312 late records were retained and included on the next compaction.
- The correction was exactly 312 records: 39,033 − 38,721 = 312, or approximately 0.8%.

The defect is therefore premature finalization/publication, not data loss.

Assertions that should gate the fix

1. Completion timing

For every window:

    completion_time >= window_end + configured_lateness_allowance

For this case, completion must not be final before 90 seconds after 14:10.

2. Inclusion at the cutoff

Every record accepted with arrival time at or before:

    window_end + 90 seconds

must be included in the final aggregate for that window.

Test both boundary cases explicitly:

- Arrival at 89.999 seconds: included.
- Arrival at exactly 90 seconds: included, if the contract is inclusive.
- Arrival after 90 seconds: behavior must be explicitly classified as late/excluded or revision-eligible.

3. No misleading final state

If the service must publish an earlier value for latency reasons, it must be marked provisional. A value published before the lateness cutoff must not be represented as final or complete.

4. Cross-service reconciliation

For each window, assert:

    accepted upstream records
      = included records
      + explicitly excluded records
      + records still pending within the lateness allowance

There must be no unexplained residual. Route loss, rejected records, and commit failures should remain zero or be accounted for explicitly.

5. Late-record inclusion

Inject records arriving at 31, 78, and 90 seconds after window end. The final result must include all records within the allowance, including records that arrive after an earlier provisional publication.

6. Exact aggregate reconciliation

After finalization, assert that the rollup equals a direct aggregation of all retained, accepted records belonging to the window and meeting the lateness rule. For this fixture:

    corrected_count = initial_count + late_count
                    = 38,721 + 312
                    = 39,033

7. Idempotent correction

Re-running compaction or replaying the same late records must not increase the count again. The corrected result must remain 39,033 after repeated compaction.

8. State-transition monotonicity

The window state should follow a clear rule such as:

    open → provisional → final

It must not transition to final and then silently change. If post-final revisions are allowed, they need an explicit revision/version contract and observable correction event.

9. No cross-window contamination

Late records must be assigned by event-time window exactly once. The fix must assert that records from this window neither disappear nor enter an adjacent five-minute window.

Recommended review wording for Cyrus

“The observed result violates the 90-second lateness contract because the window became final 31 seconds after its end, 59 seconds before the allowed cutoff. The 312 records arrived within the contract window—the latest at 78 seconds—and were retained, so this is premature finalization rather than upstream loss. Gate the fix on completion timing, inclusion of all records through the cutoff, accepted-to-included reconciliation, exact aggregate equality, idempotent compaction, and an explicit provisional-versus-final state.”

output.body:
# Goal
First-cut controls for the Q4 Cardinality Guardrails work; keep it tied to the September mirror/replay legacy-aggregator wobble without turning validation movement into rollback criteria.

# First-cut matrix

## 1. Label limits
- Failure mode: unbounded or newly introduced label keys/values causing fanout.
- Candidate control: a narrow allowlist or budget per sensitive label family.
- Preflight: flag new high-cardinality labels before a metrics-router or shard-keeper push.

## 2. Alert-source semantics
- Failure mode: responders treating replay/mirror validation movement as live-path rollback evidence.
- Candidate control: dashboard and alert wording that marks live metrics-router traffic separately from replay or mirror validation samples.

## 3. Label-change preflight
- Failure mode: a config or parser change adding labels without checking cardinality behavior.
- Candidate control: a pre-push checklist with sample counts, source label, owner, and rollback/non-rollback semantics.

# Non-goals
- No customer-facing dashboard.
- No general telemetry rewrite.
- No legacy-aggregator retirement claim.
- No claim that the 2% replay sample creates immediate storage savings.
- No Q3 incident framing.

# Monday questions
- What cost examples can Cyrus bring by label family?
- Which preflight checks are service-owned by Alex versus data-platform advisory?
- What would make the first cut too broad?

## Bounded observability example — exception-review outcomes

The accepted production counter uses only these bounded labels:
- `service_pair_class`: `ingest_path`, `routing_path`, `ownership_path`, or `other`
- `exception_class`: `invariant`, `provenance`, `failure_mode`, `ownership`, or `escalation`
- `outcome`: `requested`, `accepted`, or `rejected`

Raw service names, owner email addresses, pull-request identifiers, and reviewer-supplied reasons remain in logs or audit records rather than metric labels. This example creates no centralized review owner: mapped owners retain implementation, operational, release, and rollback responsibility, while boundary review remains limited to the triggered cross-service exception.

output.title: INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action
output.body:
# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.
- 09:05 ET — p99 returned to about 46 ms, error rate returned to roughly 0.02%, and dropped writes returned to zero.

## What changed
The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

## Why rollback was appropriate
The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

## Follow-ups
1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.
2. Patch the Cardinality Guardrails checklist so live-path label value-shape changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture, not only replay validation.

## Non-goals
This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.

> **Boundary:** This document defines a customer-safe contract only. It grants no customer access, does not copy the internal Lantern UI, exposes no raw internal discussion or internal permission identifiers, and is not an employee-performance or manager-readiness surface.

## Audience and non-goals

Define the intended customer audience and the operational questions the preview may answer. Record explicit non-goals, including customer access before the contract is reviewed, exposure of internal discussions or permission identifiers, employee-level operational signals, manager-readiness interpretation, and copying the internal UI.

## Tenant authorization

Specify how tenant authorization is evaluated, what tenant boundary is checked, and how unauthorized access is represented.

## External fields

### Deploy movement

Define the externally stable deployment identifier, service, environment, state transition, and customer-visible timestamp. Exclude internal actor IDs, chat links, and raw pipeline job identifiers.

### Service ownership

Define the service-facing support or escalation label. Exclude employee names and internal owner-map records.

### Incident load

Define the customer-safe operational summary, including its time window, aggregation rules, minimum threshold, and treatment of suppressed, stale, missing, delayed, and unavailable data.
