output.title: Lantern published service alias rule — May 14 decision
output.body:
# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Authority-record time semantics — March 18 brown-bag

## Authoritative source time
`source_timestamp` represents the original authoritative time of the underlying authority record. Later observation, serialization, processing, retry, and navigation times may be recorded as separate metadata, but they must not replace or refresh `source_timestamp`.

## Fail-closed behavior
If a required source timestamp is missing or malformed, downstream navigation fails closed to explicit unknown.

## Multiple authority references
When one card carries multiple authority references, each reference retains its own `source_timestamp`. An envelope time, render time, processing time, or newest retry time must not be substituted for any reference's authoritative source time.

## Unchanged boundaries
This discussion creates no ownership, implementation, release, approval, or customer-authorization change. The internal reference-only integration remains outside the Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce customer paths.

### What happened
A reassessment was completed at 16:55, and the entry documenting it was made at 17:40.

“Late entry entered at 17:40 for a reassessment performed at 16:55. This entry records the findings from the 16:55 reassessment and does not alter the earlier record.”

That the entry existed at 16:55, that documentation time was changed to match the reassessment time, or that an earlier entry was replaced.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The first run engaged the secondary at minute 47 while the cause remained unisolated, missing the required before-45-minute boundary. The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.

# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.
- 09:05 ET — p99 returned to about 46 ms, error rate returned to roughly 0.02%, and dropped writes returned to zero.

## What changed
The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

## Why rollback was appropriate
The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

## Follow-ups
1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.
2. Patch the Cardinality Guardrails checklist so live-path label value-shape changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture, not only replay validation.

## Non-goals
This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.

# Cross-service gate exceptions — June 14 review

I define cross-service gates and escalation boundaries; I do not take over routine service operation or Iris's product interpretation.

## 1. Metrics-router generation-retirement thresholds

- **Invariant:** Pause additional configuration pushes if retired objects accumulate above four or cleanup pauses exceed 100 milliseconds. Preserve rollback for active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.
- **Observed evidence:** A single-file canary reached four retired generations and a 92-millisecond cleanup pause; the values approached but did not cross the thresholds, and the other consistency, parity, drop, reload, heap, and restart checks remained clean.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The event is near the pause boundaries; it does not establish that later pushes are safe without observation.
- **Mapped owner:** Metrics-router service ownership remains with the mapped service owner; Wes is the practical first-pass backup within the existing deploy rules.
- **Decision needed:** Whether the next configuration push may proceed one at a time.
- **Escalation condition:** Cross more than four retired objects or 100 milliseconds of cleanup pause, or observe active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.

## 2. Ingest-edge bounded decompression

- **Invariant:** Keep active decompression bounded at four per pod and two per tenant; preserve permit cleanup, body limits, accepted-point integrity, request-p99 rollback gates, and randomized one-, two-, and three-second Retry-After behavior.
- **Observed evidence:** Request p99 briefly rose 19 milliseconds above baseline; decode-wait p99 reached 188 milliseconds, waiting work reached eleven on the busiest pods, and one tenant represented 64% of queued requests. Active work stayed within the per-pod and per-tenant limits, permits returned to zero, oversized bodies were rejected before over-budget append, no accepted points were dropped, and no pod restarted.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The concentrated waiting queue raises a separate fairness and capacity question even though no rollback gate fired.
- **Mapped owner:** Ingest-edge routine operation remains with its mapped service owner; cross-service gate review remains with Alex.
- **Decision needed:** Leave the bounded-decompression release in production and define the owner-led fairness or capacity follow-up.
- **Escalation condition:** A production rollback gate fires, including a permit leak, active-work limit violation, dropped accepted points, or the applicable sustained request-p99 threshold.

## 3. Lantern deploy provenance

- **Invariant:** Emit an external deploy event only when all required provenance validates; otherwise represent the result as explicit unknown with a machine-readable missing-provenance reason.
- **Observed evidence:** The corrected fixture rejects partial deploy objects, covers each missing required field with negative tests, performs authorization before lookup, and does not use internal room metadata or inferred ownership.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** Guarded internal validation is active, but customer access remains closed; no external preview access is granted by this correction.
- **Mapped owner:** Alex defines the external data and failure-mode requirements; Iris leads product interpretation.
- **Decision needed:** Approve the fail-closed correction and focused tests without broadening the external contract.
- **Escalation condition:** Any implementation emits partial provenance, consults internal-only metadata, or treats guarded internal validation as customer access.

## 4. Rollup correction backlog

- **Invariant:** Correction processing must preserve assignment epochs, complete assignment snapshots, minimum-watermark evaluation, matching checkpoints and compaction IDs, and duplicate-free publication.
- **Observed evidence:** The correction-backlog evidence is still under review.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The backlog increase must be distinguished between bounded backfill and a stuck correction loop, checkpoint mismatch, duplicate processing, or publication risk.
- **Mapped owner:** Cyrus's data-platform team retains rollup-service implementation and operational ownership.
- **Decision needed:** Decide whether the production fix remains in place and what owner-led pacing, capacity, or alert-tuning follow-up is justified.
- **Escalation condition:** Evidence of repeated processing, checkpoint or assignment mismatch, duplicate output, loss of first-pass currency, or a broken complete-assignment-snapshot gate.

output.title: Oversized-batch design and staged enablement — through January 28
output.body:
# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window
Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

## Evidence

## April 27, 2026 — Lantern authorization-before-source-access scenario

### Scenario
During the April Lantern migration preflight in staging, all 20 unauthorized lookups were ultimately denied, but every one constructed and initialized the incident-load adapter before authorization completed. Two of those 20 requests also accessed the source. This is a blocked pre-authorization candidate, not a deployed customer incident. The candidate is not deployed, and existing customer access remains unchanged.

### Expected boundary analysis
- Authorization must complete before incident-load adapter construction or source access. A final denial is insufficient if the adapter was constructed or the source was accessed first.
- Keep existing customer access unchanged while the candidate remains undeployed.
- Require denial regressions showing zero adapter constructions and zero source calls, followed by the affected LPS-001 rerun, before migration acceptance.
- Preserve the ownership boundary: Product Engineering remains the mapped implementation and release owner. Alex maintains this cross-service failure case and reviews the shared safety and failure-mode boundary; this scenario does not make Alex Product Engineering's implementation or release owner.

This case is for future quarterly incident practice under the existing module split: Wes owns and teaches responder paths, Nadia retains the postmortem section, and Alex maintains cross-service failure cases.

## October 16, 2026 — shard-keeper lease-loss and serving-gate case

### Tested staging sequence
1. The old holder closes its serving gate on lease loss.
2. The replacement remains out of routing while it catches up.
3. Routing begins only after the replacement opens its serving gate.

### Failure triggers
- Any overlapping serving holders.
- Any routing to a closed serving gate.
- Any request without exactly one terminal result.

### Role and ownership boundaries
- Wes owns and teaches the responder path.
- Nadia retains the postmortem material.
- Alex maintains only this cross-service failure case.
- Shard-keeper remains outside Wes’s solo scope.
- The clean October 16 result was a paired staging drill only; it made no production or ownership change.

## November 10, 2026 — facilitator-only timing for shard-keeper handoff exercise

### Timed inject sequence
- **T+0 — Baseline:** Present the old lease holder as serving and the replacement as catching up. Ask responders to state lease ownership, serving-gate state, routing eligibility, and request-accounting obligations separately.
- **T+4 — Lease transfer:** Transfer the lease before the replacement serving gate opens. Require responders to keep the replacement out of routing until its serving gate opens.
- **T+8 — In-flight request:** Reveal one request that the old holder accepted before lease loss and that remains in flight. Require a terminal accounting for that request independent of listener closure or current lease ownership.
- **T+12 — Listener closure prompt:** State that the old listener has closed. Ask whether that proves the accepted request reached a terminal result. Do not accept listener closure as sufficient evidence.
- **T+16 — Reconciliation:** Require a final timeline showing routing eligibility for both holders and exactly one terminal outcome for the pre-lease-loss request.

### Scoring points
Award one point for each:
1. Separating lease ownership from serving eligibility.
2. Keeping the replacement out of routing until its serving gate opens.
3. Treating old-listener closure as distinct from request completion.
4. Recording exactly one terminal outcome for the request accepted before lease loss.
5. Preserving the role and scope boundaries: Wes teaches the responder path; Nadia retains postmortem material; Alex maintains only the cross-service failure case; Cyrus covers the Data Platform boundary.

This is facilitator-only training material, not a production drill, system change, ownership change, or expansion of Wes’s solo shard-keeper scope.

The quarterly incident-practice session is complete. Participants correctly kept the replacement holder out of routing until its serving gate opened and identified that lease ownership alone did not establish serving eligibility.

In two of four response timelines, the responder initially treated closing the old listener as sufficient and omitted the terminal outcome for the request accepted before lease loss. After the facilitator inject, both responders corrected the timeline and accounted for that request exactly once. Retain this as training evidence for future responder-path practice.

This was training only. No production drill, deployment, or system change occurred. ### Timed scenario
- **T+0 — Accepted work:** State that ingest-edge has already accepted 200 requests into tenant queues. Ask responders to name the accounting obligation for all accepted work.
- **T+4 — Readiness and listener change:** Readiness turns false and the listener closes. Ask responders to separate refusal of new work from responsibility for requests already accepted.
- **T+8 — Dispatch-loop exit:** Reveal that the dispatch loop exits with 37 requests still queued, leaving only 163 terminal outcomes. Ask whether listener closure or false readiness is sufficient evidence that accepted work completed.
- **T+12 — Reconciliation:** Require responders to reconcile all 200 accepted requests without duplication and identify the missing 37 terminal outcomes.
- **T+16 — Incident clock:** If isolation has failed while the primary remains in the incident and the cause is not isolated, require engagement of the secondary before the established 45-minute boundary.

### Facilitator prompts
1. What changes for new work when readiness becomes false and the listener closes?
2. What obligation remains for the 200 requests already accepted into tenant queues?
3. Does dispatch-loop exit prove completion? If not, what terminal evidence is missing?
4. How will responders demonstrate that every accepted request either drained or received one explicit terminal result?
5. How will responders reconcile all 200 requests exactly once, without loss or duplication?
6. When does the established incident-clock rule require the secondary to be engaged if isolation fails?

### Scoring points
Award one point for each:
1. Separating refusal of new work from responsibility for accepted work.
2. Requiring every accepted request to drain or receive one explicit terminal result.
3. Reconciling all 200 accepted requests without duplication, including the 37 initially left queued.
4. Engaging the secondary before the 45-minute boundary when the primary remains in the incident and the cause is not isolated.
5. Preserving the role split: Wes teaches the responder path, Nadia reviews the postmortem section, and Alex contributes only the cross-service failure case.

A staged metrics-router replacement rollout contains ten instances compiling the 40,000-route matcher fixture. Compilation times range from 25 to 34 seconds against the deploy pipeline’s fixed 30-second readiness timeout. Eight instances become ready and join on their first attempt. # Metrics-router canary-response walkthrough — facilitator sheet

> **PROMINENT RECOVERY CALLOUT:** After a stopped window recovers, a fresh decision permits exactly one fully observed push. It does not reopen the whole window. A later multi-push window requires another separate fresh opening decision after that recovery push returns the full health set to baseline.

## 1. Opening decision versus operator actions
- Every owner-led configuration window requires a fresh opening decision from Alex.

- Retired generations must remain at four or fewer.
- Cleanup pauses must remain at or below 100 milliseconds.

- Crossing either the retired-generation or cleanup-pause threshold stops the window immediately.
- Active-generation inconsistency, route-parity failure, dropped series, reload failure, or restart remains a rollback condition.

## 4. Correct recovery sequence
1. Recover and re-establish the full health set.
2. Obtain a fresh decision for exactly one fully observed recovery push.
3. Observe that push through return of the full health set to baseline.
4. If another multi-push window is needed, obtain a separate fresh opening decision.

output.title: Lantern published service alias rule — May 14 decision
output.body:
# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Authority-record time semantics — March 18 brown-bag

## Authoritative source time
`source_timestamp` represents the original authoritative time of the underlying authority record. Later observation, serialization, processing, retry, and navigation times may be recorded as separate metadata, but they must not replace or refresh `source_timestamp`.

## Fail-closed behavior
If a required source timestamp is missing or malformed, downstream navigation fails closed to explicit unknown.

## Multiple authority references
When one card carries multiple authority references, each reference retains its own `source_timestamp`. An envelope time, render time, processing time, or newest retry time must not be substituted for any reference's authoritative source time.

## Unchanged boundaries
This discussion creates no ownership, implementation, release, approval, or customer-authorization change. The internal reference-only integration remains outside the Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce customer paths.

# October 27, 2027 facilitator packet

## Example 1 — separate reassessment time from entry time

### What happened
A reassessment was completed at 16:55, and the entry documenting it was made at 17:40.

### Safe wording
“Late entry entered at 17:40 for a reassessment performed at 16:55. This entry records the findings from the 16:55 reassessment and does not alter the earlier record.”

### What the wording must not imply
That the entry existed at 16:55, that documentation time was changed to match the reassessment time, or that an earlier entry was replaced.

## Example 2 — addendum preserving the original record

### What happened
A later review found that the original entry omitted a clarification. The original entry remains visible, and an addendum is entered at 18:10.

### Safe wording

- Keep exactly these three categories under each example: What happened; Safe wording; What the wording must not imply.
- Add no patient-specific clinical detail.

# Q4 triggered review — metrics-router cancellation terminal accounting — October 11, 2027

## Intake
- Affected component: metrics-router replacement activation
- Mapped implementation and release owner: Wes
- Exception class: `failure_mode`
- Concrete observed condition: after an activation attempt was accepted, deploy-pipeline cancellation could emit caller-visible `cancelled` while a concurrent activation worker committed publication and emitted caller-visible `published` for the same attempt.

## Initial observed evidence
Staging reproduced both caller-visible terminal outcomes in 14 of 10,000 cancellation-versus-commit interleavings.

## Passing correction evidence — October 14
Across 5,000 cancellation-versus-activation-commit races, including cancellation immediately before and after the commit boundary, every accepted attempt produced one durable attempt result and exactly one caller-visible terminal outcome.

## Passing process-crash evidence — October 26
Across 3,000 crashes before, during, and after the cancellation-versus-publication commit boundary, restart recovered one durable attempt identity and exactly one caller-visible terminal outcome for every accepted attempt. No attempt produced both `cancelled` and `published`.

## Partial disconnect evidence — November 9
Across 2,000 post-acceptance disconnect cases, the server retained one durable attempt identity and one terminal journal record with no duplicate execution. The harness did not reconnect or retry as the caller, so caller-visible recovery remained open.

## Final caller-recovery evidence — December 8
Across 2,000 post-acceptance disconnect cases, the caller reconnects or retries using the same durable attempt identity and receives the original single terminal outcome. No retry creates another attempt, re-executes accepted work, or creates a second terminal record.

## Closure
The durable-attempt identity, exactly-one terminal outcome, cancellation ordering, process-crash recovery, and caller-visible reconnect or same-attempt retry requirements are satisfied. Alex’s caller-visible terminal-outcome boundary is closed.

Wes retains implementation, release, and rollback authority. Closing Alex’s failure-mode boundary does not approve implementation or release.

output.title: Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet
output.body:
# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The first run engaged the secondary at minute 47 while the cause remained unisolated, missing the required before-45-minute boundary. The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.

pr.title: docs: add laptop fast path for urgent deploys and rollbacks
pr.author: wes
pr.body:
## Summary

Documents a faster break-glass procedure for Wes during urgent production deploy and rollback work.

## Proposed procedure

When waiting for the normal release mechanism would extend an incident, Wes may run `deployctl direct` from his maintainer laptop using production credentials. The command deploys the selected revision or restores the prior revision directly. The operator should record the incident ticket, service, revision, reason, and command output, then reconcile the resulting state with the normal release records after the incident.

## Motivation

This avoids waiting for the normal release job during time-sensitive recovery while retaining an audit trail in the incident record.

## Review question

Are the logging and post-incident reconciliation steps sufficient for this urgent path?

Classification: localized tenant-specific queueing/backpressure, not yet a demonstrated scheduler-fairness failure or fleet-wide ingest-edge incident.

The evidence against a broad scheduler failure is:

- Dispatch errors and accepted-point accounting are normal.
- Other tenants are unaffected.
- The tenant is below its eight-request waiting cap.
- There is no current evidence of empty tenants remaining in the round-robin ring.

However, seven queued requests and a 2.6-second queue-wait p99 are enough to investigate before changing anything. Do not raise the cap or alter scheduling yet.

Smallest evidence set

1. Trace a small request sample

For 3–5 affected-tenant requests, plus one request from an unaffected tenant, capture one correlated trace containing:

- Client request start and declared deadline.
- Ingest-edge receive/admission time.
- Waiting-queue enqueue time.
- Tenant-ring insertion and each scheduler turn considered.
- Pod and tenant active counts at each skipped turn.
- Actual permit reservation and dequeue time.
- Decompression/handler start and completion.
- Response-write completion.
- Client cancellation, disconnect, or timeout time and reason.

Use request IDs and a bounded tenant identifier; do not add raw unbounded tenant labels to metrics.

The decisive scheduler fields are: “was the request eligible?”, “was a pod slot available?”, and “did the ring advance past it or contain stale/empty entries?”

2. Check the timeout boundary

For the same traces, compare:

- Client deadline origin: request creation, connection acquisition, or only server submission.
- Client cancellation timestamp.
- Gateway/proxy timeout.
- Ingest-edge server timeout.
- Handler completion timestamp.
- Response-write/reset timestamp.

A client-timeout explanation is supported if the client deadline expires before or near handler/response completion, especially when the request’s actual ingest-edge queue wait is materially smaller than the end-to-end elapsed time. Reproduce once with a controlled client using a longer deadline and connection reuse, without changing ingest-edge.

3. Check queue age against eligibility

For the incident window, retrieve only:

- Affected tenant queue depth.
- Oldest waiting-request age.
- Per-request queue wait for the sampled traces.
- Scheduler dispatch turns and ring contents.
- Pod active count versus the four-active limit.
- Affected-tenant active count versus the two-active limit.
- Any cancellation/removal events.

Interpretation:

- Fairness/work-conservation failure: a live request remains queued while it is eligible, a pod slot is genuinely available, and the scheduler skips it or waits for a later ring rebuild; stale empty tenants or a non-advancing ring appear in the same interval.
- Expected tenant backpressure: the pod is at four active, or the tenant is at two active, or the request is correctly waiting behind eligible work; queue age tracks actual permit occupancy.
- Client-held-open/timeout behavior: requests are canceled or held until the client deadline, while server-side queue/dispatch timing is normal; handler or connection time consumes most of the deadline.
- Cancellation cleanup issue: client cancellations remove the request from the tenant queue but the tenant remains in the ring, or queue depth/ring membership diverges.

Decision: keep ingest-edge unchanged unless the trace proves an eligible request was skipped while capacity was idle, or proves stale empty tenants/ring advancement caused the wait. results.content:
Review verdict: not implementation-ready yet.

The active limits are clear and should remain:

- Maximum 4 active decompressions per pod.
- Maximum 2 active decompressions per tenant.
- These are hard invariants, including during cancellation, failure, and scheduler races.

The missing behavior should be specified as follows.

1. Queue and scheduling model

Define an explicit global waiting-capacity limit, G. A per-tenant limit of 8 alone is not a global bound if many tenants enqueue simultaneously.

Use:

- One FIFO subqueue per tenant.
- A round-robin ring of tenants whose subqueues are nonempty.
- A request gets at most one dispatch per tenant turn.
- New requests join the tail of their tenant’s subqueue; they must not bypass older requests from that tenant.
- When a tenant is served, it moves to the back of the tenant ring if it still has live requests.
- Empty tenants are removed from the ring.
- Canceled entries are removed or treated as tombstones and skipped before dispatch.

The scheduler must be work-conserving: whenever a live queued request is eligible and a pod slot is available, it should dispatch without waiting for unrelated queue activity.

Eligibility requires both:

- Pod active count < 4.
- That tenant’s active count < 2.

A tenant at its active limit must be skipped, not allowed to block other tenants. It remains in the ring and becomes eligible again when one of its active requests reaches a terminal state.

The pod and tenant active reservations must be made at one linearization point. Do not dequeue a request and then separately acquire permits in a way that allows over-admission or head-of-line blocking. The scheduler should either:

- Reserve both counters under one scheduler lock, or
- Acquire both non-blockingly and roll back the first reservation if the second cannot be acquired.

Never hold a pod/global permit while waiting for a tenant permit.

2. Request lifecycle and cancellation

Document the state machine:

received → waiting → active → terminal

Cancellation may transition:

- waiting → canceled
- active → cancellation requested → terminal

Required behavior:

- A waiting cancellation removes the request from its tenant queue, decrements the live waiting count exactly once, and wakes the scheduler.
- A canceled waiting request must never be dispatched or decompressed.
- If dispatch and cancellation race, exactly one wins the waiting-to-active transition.
- If dispatch wins, cancellation follows active-request cleanup rules; if cancellation wins, no active permit may be acquired.
- Active cancellation releases both pod and tenant reservations exactly once when the decoder actually stops or reaches its terminal cleanup path.
- Decoder failure, timeout, body-limit rejection, client cancellation, and successful completion must all use the same single-cleanup guard.
- Queue capacity must be released when a request leaves the waiting queue, not when downstream processing completes.
- Active capacity must be released when active decompression terminates.

Use an O(1) queue handle for removal if possible. If tombstones are used instead, the live-count decrement and tombstone state transition must still be idempotent.

3. Capacity sharing

Use a shared global waiting pool of G slots plus a hard per-tenant waiting cap of 8.

The intended semantics should be:

- A tenant may hold at most 8 waiting requests.
- Unused capacity is not reserved for inactive tenants.
- Any tenant below 8 may use any available global slot.
- No tenant may exceed 8 merely because other tenants are idle.
- If the global pool is full, reject even if the submitting tenant has fewer than 8 waiting requests.
- If that tenant’s cap is full, reject even if global slots remain.
- Enqueue and capacity reservation must be atomic with respect to dequeue, cancellation, and other submitters.
- No request may consume both a waiting slot and an active slot simultaneously.

This gives borrowing without allowing one tenant to monopolize the queue. If the requirement is that every tenant must retain capacity under global saturation, that is a different design requiring explicit reserved floors or weighted partitions; it should not be implied by “borrowing.”

Admission must recover one-for-one as slots are released. There must be no stale full flag, manual reset, lost wakeup, deadlock, or capacity leak.

Record separate rejection reasons for:

- Tenant waiting cap reached.
- Global waiting cap reached.
- Any separate active/decompression admission rejection.

4. Retry-After behavior

Preserve the established ingest-edge behavior:

- Return HTTP 429 when the tenant waiting cap or global waiting cap rejects a request.
- Include a valid randomized Retry-After value of 1, 2, or 3 seconds on every such response.
- Treat the value as the minimum retry delay, not as a promise that the next attempt will succeed.
- Generate and validate the header per response; do not return a fixed value or omit it on one overload path.
- Do not change the existing randomized range as part of this scheduler work.
- Do not return 429 for malformed encoding, decompressed-body-limit violations, or other permanent request errors; those retain their existing error semantics.
- A client cancellation should terminate the request rather than be converted into a server-generated 429.

Tests should verify range, presence, and per-response behavior, without asserting a particular random sequence.

5. Starvation and fairness requirements

Strict round-robin should be defined in terms of dispatch turns:

- With N nonempty, eligible tenant queues, the scheduler dispatches at most one request for a tenant before giving other eligible tenants their turns.
- A tenant that remains continuously nonempty and eligible cannot be skipped indefinitely.
- Between two dispatches for one tenant, no more than N−1 other tenant turns may occur, excluding canceled or currently ineligible tenants.
- A newly arriving tenant joins at the current ring tail; it must not reset the round-robin pointer.
- A tenant at active count 2 is temporarily ineligible, not starved; when its permit is released it re-enters at the next appropriate turn.
- If only one tenant has live work, it may use its available tenant capacity, but still cannot exceed two active requests.
- Queue fairness is per request. If decompression cost varies substantially by payload, measure decode time and queue age separately; request round-robin is not a guarantee of equal CPU consumption.

The known failure mode here is concentrated waiting work despite active limits holding: prior evidence showed one tenant representing 64% of queued requests while the 4-per-pod and 2-per-tenant active limits remained intact. The implementation must therefore prove waiting-time fairness, not merely active-count isolation.

6. Focused tests required before approval

Concurrency and invariants

- Many concurrent submitters never produce more than 4 active decompressions per pod.
- No tenant ever exceeds 2 active decompressions.
- The global waiting count never exceeds G.
- A tenant never exceeds 8 waiting requests.
- Dequeue versus enqueue has one unambiguous linearization point.
- Simultaneous releases and submissions cannot overfill the queue.
- Admission resumes automatically after one, several, and all available slots are released.

Round-robin behavior

- Two tenants produce A1, B1, A2, B2 ordering while both remain eligible.
- Three tenants produce one turn per tenant.
- A tenant with a full active limit is skipped while another eligible tenant proceeds.
- Empty tenants, canceled entries, and newly arriving tenants do not corrupt ring order.
- A continuously flooded tenant cannot prevent a second tenant from being dispatched.

Capacity sharing

- One tenant can use otherwise idle global capacity up to its limit of 8.
- Multiple tenants can share the global pool without exceeding either their individual caps or G.
- An idle tenant’s unused nominal capacity is borrowable.
- Global-full and tenant-full conditions return distinct rejection reasons and both return HTTP 429 with the existing Retry-After behavior.
- A canceled waiting request immediately makes its slot available to another request.

Cancellation and cleanup

Test cancellation:

- Before queue admission.
- While waiting in the tenant queue.
- During a dequeue/dispatch race.
- After pod reservation but before tenant reservation, if the implementation has staged acquisition.
- During active decompression.
- After partial output.
- During decoder failure or timeout cleanup.

Every case must prove:

- No canceled request is decompressed or written downstream.
- No permit or queue slot is leaked.
- No permit is released twice.
- Counts return to their pre-test values.
- The queue drains fully after the workload ends.

Run a repeated cancellation stress test, including the existing 10,000-cancellation regression case.

Starvation and latency

- Flood tenant A while continuously submitting work for tenants B and C.
- Assert B and C receive service within the declared bounded-turn criterion.
- Use fixed-duration decoders for a deterministic wall-clock bound, then separately test variable decode durations.
- Measure and report per-tenant queue age and decode-wait p50/p95/p99.
- Verify ordinary traffic remains responsive under decompression-heavy traffic.
- Verify a burst drains and returns to baseline within a declared recovery interval.

Retry and error semantics

- Every queue-capacity 429 has Retry-After of exactly 1, 2, or 3 seconds.
- Retry-After remains randomized across repeated responses.
- Body-limit, malformed-input, decoder-failure, and cancellation outcomes are not misclassified as queue-capacity 429s.
- No accepted points are dropped, duplicated, or written after cancellation.

Observability

Expose separate metrics for:

- Waiting requests, by bounded tenant classification if tenant labels are permitted.
- Oldest queue age.
- Decode wait duration.
- Active decompressions per pod.
- Active decompressions per tenant.
- Global and per-tenant queue-cap rejections.
- Cancellations, decoder failures, and cleanup failures.
- Permit and queue-slot high-water marks.

Do not add raw tenant IDs or request IDs as unbounded metric labels.

Implementation gate

Do not begin implementation until Wes adds:

1. The global waiting-capacity value and its sizing rationale.
2. The exact enqueue/dequeue/cancellation linearization rules.
3. The scheduler ring semantics, including ineligible tenants.
4. The one-time cleanup ownership for every terminal path.
5. The Retry-After contract.
6. A deterministic starvation bound and test plan.
7. The focused concurrency, cancellation, capacity-sharing, and regression tests above.

The proposal is directionally sound, but “tenant round-robin plus eight waiting requests” is not sufficient by itself. The safety properties are the atomic reservation rules, exact cancellation cleanup, an explicit global queue bound, and measurable starvation guarantees.

input.body:
Request changes: this redesign is not safe for production dispatch.

1. Removing the per-tenant waiting cap breaks the standing production contract: each tenant may have at most 8 accepted waiting requests, with excess requests rejected before acceptance as HTTP 429 with the existing randomized Retry-After (1–3 seconds). Without that bound, one noisy tenant can consume unbounded accepted queue/memory and starve other tenants. Keep the tenant cap and add/retain an explicit bounded global waiting pool with atomic admission and distinct tenant-full/global-full rejection reasons.

2. A single request FIFO reintroduces head-of-line blocking and loses tenant fairness. If the FIFO head belongs to a tenant already at the 2-active-per-tenant limit, an eligible request from another tenant behind it cannot use an available pod slot. Production dispatch must use per-tenant FIFO subqueues plus a round-robin ring of nonempty tenants, skip temporarily ineligible tenants, and remain work-conserving. Preserve the hard limit of 4 active decompressions per pod and 2 per tenant.

3. Delaying insertion into runnable scheduling state until a worker is free must not hide accepted waiting requests from queue accounting, cancellation, age/occupancy observability, or fairness. Define the received → waiting → active → terminal state transitions and make enqueue/dequeue/cancellation linearizable; a waiting cancellation must free its slot exactly once and wake dispatch, while a dispatch/cancellation race must result in exactly one winner.

Please revise the implementation and add focused tests for: noisy-tenant flooding with bounded service for other tenants; two-/three-tenant round-robin order; skipping an at-limit tenant while another proceeds; tenant and global capacity limits and recovery; cancellation/dispatch races and the existing 10,000-cancellation regression; exactly-one terminal result per accepted request; active-count invariants; and 429 Retry-After presence/range on every queue-capacity rejection. Do not roll this to production until those invariants and accepted-point accounting are demonstrated.

pr.title: Resolve historical owner-map aliases

changed_files.summary: The resolver iterates owner-map alias rows in storage order. For rows matching the tenant and historical identifier, it returns the first row whose effective_start <= source_event_timestamp <= effective_end, using that row's canonical_service_id. If no interval match is found, it selects a canonical service in the same tenant using normalized service-name similarity.

pr.diff_summary: Overlapping active aliases are resolved by the first matching record in storage order. When no interval match exists, the patch infers a rename from similar service names.

input.body:
Request changes. This does not match Lantern’s established service-identity rule:

- Resolution must evaluate every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp; it must not return the first match in storage order.
- If qualifying aliases identify different canonical published services, the resolver must fail closed: keep the signals separate and render ownership as explicit unknown, independent of storage order.
- If no qualifying alias exists, it must also keep the signals separate and render explicit unknown. It must never infer a rename from normalized/similar service names or customer context.

Please add regression coverage for both row orders of conflicting overlaps, both inclusive endpoints, a single valid match, out-of-interval/no-alias fallback, and the no-heuristic-inference case.

results.content:
Ten-minute spoken outline

0:00–1:00 — The rule in one sentence

“Effective April 7, every cross-service proposal names its ordinary implementation and release owner, plus any boundary-specific exception reviewer. The key distinction is that exception review is scoped to the exception; it is not a new centralized approval layer.”

1:00–2:30 — What stays with the mapped owner

“The mapped owner still owns the normal work: implementation, operational readiness, release or go/no-go, and—where applicable—rollback. Naming an exception reviewer does not move those responsibilities to Infra, to me, or to any other central function.”

2:30–4:00 — The Lantern example

“The completed Lantern incident-load migration is a useful example. Product Engineering owned the implementation and retained release ownership. Iris retained responsibility for customer interpretation—what the resulting incident-load explanation means for the customer and how it is presented.”

4:00–6:00 — What triggered the exception review

“The migration moved an existing incident-load source into shared registration, so it crossed the shared-registration safety boundary. That triggered a bounded review of the relevant safety and failure modes: authorization before source access, provenance and timestamp handling, explicit unknown for stale or missing input, excluded-field protection, and preservation of read-only behavior.”

6:00–7:30 — My role

“My role was only to review that triggered shared-registration safety and failure-mode boundary. I checked whether the boundary conditions were satisfied and whether any failure mode required correction or escalation. I did not become the implementation owner, the customer-interpretation owner, or the ordinary release approver.”

7:30–9:00 — What the model does not mean

“So the workflow was not: Product Engineering builds something, then waits for a centralized Infra approval. It was: Product Engineering builds and releases within its mapped ownership; Iris handles the customer interpretation; and the named exception reviewer examines only the specific boundary that was triggered.”

9:00–10:00 — Close with the operating pattern

“The practical pattern is simple: ordinary work stays with the mapped owner; a defined exception routes to the person accountable for that boundary; and once the boundary is resolved, the work returns to the ordinary owner-led path. An exception reviewer adds clarity and safety coverage—it does not create a centralized approval gate or transfer ordinary implementation and release authority.”

sources.label: Assistant's reply to Alex Valdez, message 002009
excerpts:
Assessment: the evidence closes the two core unit-level concerns, but it is not yet the accepted blocker-clearing result.

What the reports establish

- Delayed-source behavior:
  - Provenance was beyond the freshness limit.
  - The stale cache entry was deleted on read.
  - The response was exactly `UNKNOWN_STALE_SOURCE`.
  - `render` was not called.
- Tenant isolation:
  - Tenant A and B used distinct cache tuples.
  - No cross-tenant object material was observed.

Those are strong positive results. They do not yet prove the complete read-path, invalidation, race, authorization, or customer-contract behavior required for closure.

Remaining checks

1. Complete Tuesday’s witnessed combined run

The run must exercise the stale-source and two-tenant cases together, with deterministic fixture resets and recorded trace correlation.

It must verify:

- A warm stale cache hit returns exactly `UNKNOWN_STALE_SOURCE`.
- The stale object cannot escape through a response, fallback, error envelope, or alternate resolver.
- The stale object cannot render on a repeated request after invalidation.
- Invalidation is scoped to the requesting tenant and cache tuple.
- A stale read cannot delete a newer object written concurrently; deletion must be version/provenance conditional or otherwise race-safe.
- When the permitted source becomes fresh, the next request follows the absent-entry fetch path and only the newly validated fresh object can render.
- Freshness is calculated from source provenance, not cache insertion time, worker heartbeat, or render time.
- Boundary cases are covered: exactly at the limit, just beyond the limit, missing provenance, and malformed provenance.
- Tenant order is reversed:
  - A populates, B reads.
  - B populates, A reads.
- The run includes one tenant stale and the other fresh.
- `get`, `set`, and `invalidate` are all exercised, not only cache reads.
- Concurrent same-service requests do not reuse the other tenant’s cache entry.
- Authorization precedes cache reads, source lookup, freshness evaluation, and rendering.
- Denied requests produce the established `403 not_authorized` result with zero cache, source-adapter, and render access.
- The tenant correlation remains consistent across authorization, cache events, adapter calls, and rendered responses.
- Rendered output contains only the requesting tenant’s fixture.

2. Complete Iris’s customer-facing wording verification

Iris must approve the exact external wording and confirm that it:

- Describes the stale permitted source as unavailable/unknown rather than current.
- Does not expose the stale object, counts, internal identifiers, cache details, or other internal provenance.
- Does not imply that stale data was successfully served.
- Preserves the distinction between source freshness and worker/cache activity.
- Does not broaden Lantern’s signal set or imply customer-preview approval.

3. Record the accepted closeout result

The blocker-clearing record must attach the witnessed run evidence, including fixture IDs, trace/correlation evidence, exact response values, render/no-render results, invalidation behavior, tenant-isolation assertions, authorization ordering, and Iris’s wording signoff.

Disposition now: blocker still open. The two fixture reports materially advance the fix and appear to pass their headline assertions, but Tuesday’s combined witnessed evidence and Iris’s wording approval remain mandatory. Customer access stays closed until both are accepted and recorded; even then, this clears the freshness blocker only and does not by itself authorize customer access.

sources.label: Assistant's reply to Alex Valdez, message 003182
excerpts:
Recommended replacement wording:

Alert source and classification

- Every signal must carry explicit `environment` and `source` labels: `production/live`, `staged/live-canary`, or `replay/validation`.
- Live production or live-canary movement is eligible for the normal production rollback/page path.
- Replay or validation movement is evidence about the test or rollout stage only. It may stop that replay or staged activity, but it must not be rendered, routed, or described as a production incident or production page.
- The queue control described here is not active enforcement on the live production path. It is a replay/staged-test control and must not be presented as a production safeguard.

Five-minute stop semantics

Treat the two conditions independently and use OR semantics:

- Stop the current test or rollout stage if `queue_wait_p99_ms > 400` continuously for five minutes.
- Stop the current test or rollout stage if `retryable_queue_full_ratio > 0.005` continuously for five minutes.
- Either sustained condition is sufficient; do not average, combine, or allow one metric to mask the other.
- “Continuously for five minutes” means the condition must remain above its threshold for the full five-minute hold. If it drops below the threshold before five minutes, that hold resets.
- Once either condition fires, freeze further exposure/enqueueing for the current stage and record the source classification, environment, start time, and firing condition. Clearing the metric does not automatically resume the test.

Routing and ownership

- Nadia retains ownership of the alert definition, source classification, routing, and alert-semantic changes.
- For `source=replay` or `source=validation`, route the stop to the replay/staged-test owner as a validation stop, not to the production paging path.
- For `source=live` in production, retain the existing production-page and rollback semantics.
- The rule must preserve the source label in the alert payload; it must not collapse replay and live signals into one service-wide alert.

Cause versus symptom wording

Use the causal condition as the primary explanation:

“Queue saturation is the suspected cause: queue wait p99 exceeded 400 ms for five minutes, or retryable queue-full ratio exceeded 0.5% for five minutes.”

Describe retryable refusal as the observed symptom, not as the cause:

“Retryable queue-full responses are the observed symptom of admission pressure; they are not evidence by themselves that the live production queue-control mechanism is active.”

For a replay firing:

“Replay validation stopped because the queue-saturation threshold was sustained for five minutes. This is a replay/staged-test stop signal, not a production page and not evidence of live production impact.”

For a live firing:

“Live traffic met the queue-saturation stop condition for five minutes. Stop the current rollout stage and follow the existing production rollback/page procedure.”

The key correction is to keep the hard-stop behavior identical for the active test or rollout stage while making the consequence source-aware: replay can stop replay, but replay cannot page production.

entries.title: April 18 outage: initial detection
entries.body: TODO: Document the first observable signal and distinguish detection symptoms from cause-specific alerting.

input.body:
April 18, 2023 outage detection

- First observable signal: 2023-04-18 21:42:00 EDT (UTC−04:00), when the shard-keeper page fired. This is the first signal recorded in the incident sequence; it is not the 18:05 EDT shard-keeper config-push completion, whose initial dashboards were green.
- Source: the operational shard-keeper page / incident sequence for INC-2023-04-18-001.
- Alerts that fired: the symptom alerts for impaired/generic ingestion behavior; the shard-keeper page was the explicit page noted at 21:42 EDT.
- Alerts that did not fire: the expected cause-specific alerts for the underlying cross-service mismatch. No alert identified the label-name change or the fact that rollup-service had not consumed it.
- What the later diagnosis showed: the initial pages looked like generic ingest weirdness, and a network-layer issue was a red herring. The later diagnosis found that Nadia’s label-name change had reached shard-keeper in the earlier config push but had not been picked up by rollup-service—a shard-keeper/rollup-service parity gap. That mismatch impaired ingestion for hours; symptom alerts fired while the cause alerts stayed silent, which slowed diagnosis.

Operational distinction: treat the first page and symptom alerts as detection signals, not as proof of the cause. Verify producer/consumer label parity and downstream rollup-service consumption before attributing a similar incident to network or generic ingestion failure.

output.body:
# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.
- 09:05 ET — p99 returned to about 46 ms, error rate returned to roughly 0.02%, and dropped writes returned to zero.

## What changed
The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

## Why rollback was appropriate
The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

## Follow-ups
1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.
2. Patch the Cardinality Guardrails checklist so live-path label value-shape changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture, not only replay validation.

## Non-goals
This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.

# Cross-service gate exceptions — June 14 review

I define cross-service gates and escalation boundaries; I do not take over routine service operation or Iris's product interpretation.

## 1. Metrics-router generation-retirement thresholds

- **Invariant:** Pause additional configuration pushes if retired objects accumulate above four or cleanup pauses exceed 100 milliseconds. Preserve rollback for active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.
- **Observed evidence:** A single-file canary reached four retired generations and a 92-millisecond cleanup pause; the values approached but did not cross the thresholds, and the other consistency, parity, drop, reload, heap, and restart checks remained clean.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The event is near the pause boundaries; it does not establish that later pushes are safe without observation.
- **Mapped owner:** Metrics-router service ownership remains with the mapped service owner; Wes is the practical first-pass backup within the existing deploy rules.
- **Decision needed:** Whether the next configuration push may proceed one at a time.
- **Escalation condition:** Cross more than four retired objects or 100 milliseconds of cleanup pause, or observe active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.

## 2. Ingest-edge bounded decompression

- **Invariant:** Keep active decompression bounded at four per pod and two per tenant; preserve permit cleanup, body limits, accepted-point integrity, request-p99 rollback gates, and randomized one-, two-, and three-second Retry-After behavior.
- **Observed evidence:** Request p99 briefly rose 19 milliseconds above baseline; decode-wait p99 reached 188 milliseconds, waiting work reached eleven on the busiest pods, and one tenant represented 64% of queued requests. Active work stayed within the per-pod and per-tenant limits, permits returned to zero, oversized bodies were rejected before over-budget append, no accepted points were dropped, and no pod restarted.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The concentrated waiting queue raises a separate fairness and capacity question even though no rollback gate fired.
- **Mapped owner:** Ingest-edge routine operation remains with its mapped service owner; cross-service gate review remains with Alex.
- **Decision needed:** Leave the bounded-decompression release in production and define the owner-led fairness or capacity follow-up.
- **Escalation condition:** A production rollback gate fires, including a permit leak, active-work limit violation, dropped accepted points, or the applicable sustained request-p99 threshold.

## 3. Lantern deploy provenance

- **Invariant:** Emit an external deploy event only when all required provenance validates; otherwise represent the result as explicit unknown with a machine-readable missing-provenance reason.
- **Observed evidence:** The corrected fixture rejects partial deploy objects, covers each missing required field with negative tests, performs authorization before lookup, and does not use internal room metadata or inferred ownership.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** Guarded internal validation is active, but customer access remains closed; no external preview access is granted by this correction.
- **Mapped owner:** Alex defines the external data and failure-mode requirements; Iris leads product interpretation.
- **Decision needed:** Approve the fail-closed correction and focused tests without broadening the external contract.
- **Escalation condition:** Any implementation emits partial provenance, consults internal-only metadata, or treats guarded internal validation as customer access.

## 4. Rollup correction backlog

- **Invariant:** Correction processing must preserve assignment epochs, complete assignment snapshots, minimum-watermark evaluation, matching checkpoints and compaction IDs, and duplicate-free publication.
- **Observed evidence:** The correction-backlog evidence is still under review.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The backlog increase must be distinguished between bounded backfill and a stuck correction loop, checkpoint mismatch, duplicate processing, or publication risk.

   - Do not infer values or use an internal fallback.

3. **Stale permitted source**
   - Return an explicit unknown with the source state represented.
   - Do not return counts or active minutes, and do not use an internal fallback.

4. **Malformed permitted source**
   - Return an explicit unknown.
   - No protected fields may enter the rendered object.

5. **Unauthorized request for each lookup type**
   - Return `403 not_authorized`.
   - Authorization must complete before any source adapter is invoked.

## Evidence requirements

Capture the external response for every case, the adapter-call trace, the source timestamp where applicable, and proof that forbidden fields do not enter the rendered object.

Keep response-content assertions separate from call-order evidence. A response that contains no protected value is not sufficient to pass an unauthorized case if a source adapter was invoked before authorization completed.

## Gate interpretation

This suite is an internal readiness check. Passing individual cases does not itself grant customer access; the preview remains internal unless the applicable readiness and access decision is made separately.

output.title: Oversized-batch design and staged enablement — through January 28
output.body:
# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window
Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

Nadia owns this front-door check. If any one of the four items is absent, including when the condition is only placeholder text such as `needs review` or `possible risk`, she returns the request to the mapped owner without review. A complete request goes to the named owner for its one selected boundary. Alex receives it only when that boundary requires his review, and he reviews only that boundary. Nadia does not make implementation, release, or rollback decisions; those decisions remain with the mapped owner.

## Scenario scope
